source: Naeini, Saqur, Saeidi, Giorgi, Taati (2023) Large Language Models are Fixated by Red Herrings: Only Connect Wall dataset
finding: First direct test of red-herring fixation (Einstellung, Smith and Blankenship style) in LLMs. Only Connect walls have 16 clues, 4 hidden groups, and built-in decoys that fit a wrong group. Models are far below humans when decoys are present.
numbers: Test set 494 walls / 1976 groups. Humans solved 285 of 494 walls (57.7%) and 1405 of 1976 groups (71.1%). GPT-4 0-shot solved 6 walls and 239 groups (12.1%); GPT-3.5-turbo 0 walls, 114 groups at 0-shot. GPT-4 clustering scores 0-shot: FMS 41.5, ARI 27.2, NMI 30.7.
limits: Human data come from show contestants under time pressure; no matched human fixation manipulation. Many clues need niche cultural knowledge, so knowledge gaps are confounded with fixation.
agent_relevance: Decoy-rich problems are a clean fixation test for an agent: S1 should name the plausible-but-wrong grouping, not just the first one.

source: Naeini, Saqur, Saeidi, Giorgi, Taati (2023) Large Language Models are Fixated by Red Herrings: Only Connect Wall dataset
finding: Dose-response test of the red herring hypothesis. Removing decoys (random re-pairing of groups, or WordNet-built walls with no decoys) raises model scores sharply. This supports decoy retrieval, not raw knowledge, as the failure cause.
numbers: GPT-4 0-shot walls solved: 6 (original) -> 59 (OCW-Randomized, 595 groups) -> 471 (OCW-WordNet, 1926 of 1976 groups = 97.5%). GPT-3.5-turbo 0-shot: 0 -> 5 -> 337 walls (1522 groups).
quote: performance increasing significantly with the reduction of red herrings from the test set
limits: WordNet walls are also semantically easier (hypernym/synonym groups), so decoy removal and easier categories are confounded. No human data on the synthetic sets.
agent_relevance: Strong evidence that distractor strength, not model knowledge, drives the gap. Argues for a step that lists rival groupings and tests each before committing.

source: Naeini, Saqur, Saeidi, Giorgi, Taati (2023) Large Language Models are Fixated by Red Herrings: Only Connect Wall dataset
finding: More in-context examples did not help grouping; the authors argue examples only teach the output format and may themselves act as red herrings. Connection naming stays far below humans.
numbers: GPT-4 grouping, correct groups: 0-shot 239, 1-shot 262, 3-shot 272, 5-shot 269, 10-shot 249 (no monotone gain). Connection naming: human about 80% correct; best model (GPT-4, 10-shot) 41-45% F1; exact match under 15%. 8.2% of best-model connections wrongly included the clues.
limits: No chain-of-thought or tree-of-thoughts run; authors leave that to future work. Exact-match metric is harsh.
agent_relevance: Few-shot demos alone do not break fixation. Reframing needs an operator, not just more examples (O6 as an operator, not a prompt hint).

source: Tian, Ravichander, Qin, Le Bras, Marjieh, Peng, Choi, Griffiths, Brahman (2023/2025) MacGyver: Are LLMs Creative Problem Solvers?
finding: Benchmark built around functional fixedness: everyday problems where the obvious use of each tool fails and a non-obvious use works. Humans and LLMs both find it hard, in different ways.
numbers: 1,683 generated problems; 1,306 human-checked (1,073 solvable, 233 unsolvable). Over 82% of solvable problems need unconventional tool use. 7 LLMs tested (Llama2 7B/13B/70B, GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Claude2 and others).
limits: Problems are text-only and LLM-generated then human-filtered, so they may carry LLM style. Human sample is crowd workers, not matched experts.
agent_relevance: Gives a ready-made functional-fixedness set to test an S1/O6 'redescribe the object by what it can do' step.

source: Tian, Ravichander, Qin, Le Bras, Marjieh, Peng, Choi, Griffiths, Brahman (2023/2025) MacGyver: Are LLMs Creative Problem Solvers?
finding: Humans beat GPT-4 on majority-correct, but GPT-4 is slightly better on a single average attempt. Humans are bimodal (perfect or total failure); GPT-4 is spread in the middle.
numbers: Average human total correct rate 65.1%. Majority-vote correct: humans 79.3% vs GPT-4 73.3%. GPT-4 and Claude2 have about 35-42% chance of a correct answer per single try. Scale alone did not unlock creative problem solving across Llama2 7b/13b/70b.
quote: average person with total correct rate of 65.1%
limits: Single-run LLM sampling at T=0.7. Authors tie the human average gap to functional fixedness, but this is an interpretation, not a manipulation.
agent_relevance: Variance profile suggests sampling many diverse attempts then checking feasibility by code helps. Matches G4: samples are not independent, so diversity must be forced.

source: Tian, Ravichander, Qin, Le Bras, Marjieh, Peng, Choi, Griffiths, Brahman (2023/2025) MacGyver: Are LLMs Creative Problem Solvers?
finding: Error analysis of GPT-4 shows the main failure is physically infeasible steps, more than fixation on the usual use. Two prompt scaffolds help: iterative step-wise self-reflection and divergent-then-convergent thinking.
numbers: Error shares: wrong tool use 42.4%, not achieving goal 17.7%, unnecessary steps 16.9%, unavailable tools 9.5% (26.4% unfaithful to constraints). On 180 solvable problems: Self-Reflect cut infeasible answers by 9.7 points and Div-Conv by 4.3; Div-Conv raised efficient solutions by 6.5 points, Self-Reflect by 2.2. Claude2 and Llama2-13b did not improve with Self-Reflect.
limits: Small gains, zero-shot, one run, one model for the main numbers. Self-reflection helped only the strongest model.
agent_relevance: Divergent list then convergent feasibility check is already a cheap O6 variant. The feasibility check must be code or a grounded checker (G2) since small models cannot self-reflect.

source: Chen, Zhu, Huang, Wang (2026) MedEinst: Benchmarking the Einstellung Effect in Medical LLMs through Counterfactual Differential Diagnosis
finding: Counterfactual paired cases: a control case and a 'trap' case with one discriminative fact changed so the common diagnosis becomes wrong. Bias Trap Rate = chance of failing the trap despite solving the control. Frontier models show high trap rates.
numbers: 5,383 paired cases, 49 diseases, 17 LLMs. Bias Trap Rate: Gemini-2.5-Pro 60.90%, Claude-Sonnet-4.5 42.98%. Qwen3-32B base baseline accuracy 40.25%. Authors report no meaningful link between model size and robustness.
limits: Cases built and checked by an LLM judge committee (96.1% passed review). Table columns in the PDF text are misaligned, so some per-model rows are uncertain. Single preprint.
agent_relevance: The paired control/trap design is a model for our own test: same problem with and without the fixation lure.

source: Chen, Zhu, Huang, Wang (2026) MedEinst: Benchmarking the Einstellung Effect in Medical LLMs through Counterfactual Differential Diagnosis
finding: Failure modes of reasoning models on the Einstellung trap: ignoring the key fact, too little reasoning, or reasoning that defends the wrong prior. Multi-agent role setups did not fix it and reinforced the dominant prior.
numbers: GPT-5 error cases: blindness (missed key evidence) over 35%; among cases where key symptoms were noticed, 43% underthinking and 22% overthinking (motivated reasoning). Agents MDAgent and DyLAN (Qwen3-32B): robust accuracy about 8-10% by the authors' text, trap rate about 40-42%.
limits: Failure mode split comes from an LLM judge over one model's errors.
agent_relevance: Supports G4/G5: agreement among samples or role-debate can lock in the shared prior. Verification must come from evidence, not votes.

source: Chen, Zhu, Huang, Wang (2026) MedEinst: Benchmarking the Einstellung Effect in Medical LLMs through Counterfactual Differential Diagnosis
finding: ECR-Agent, an evidence-checking agent loop (dynamic causal graph, evidence audit, critic-driven memory), lowers the trap rate and raises accuracy over its Qwen3-32B base.
numbers: Qwen3-32B base baseline accuracy 40.25%; adding the causal-inference module 55.49%; full ECR-Agent 69.49% baseline accuracy, 24.21% robust accuracy, 33.75% Bias Trap Rate.
limits: Authors' own agent on authors' own benchmark; code not yet released; stored cases could leak disease patterns. Trap rate still one third.
agent_relevance: Evidence that a structured 'does the discriminating fact match my hypothesis' audit helps, but not enough alone. Fits G2 and O6.

source: Kim, Podlasek, Shidara, Liu, Alaa, Bernardo (2025) Limitations of LLMs in Clinical Problem-Solving Arising from Inflexible Reasoning (M-ARC)
finding: M-ARC: 100 medical questions built to trigger Einstellung (a familiar pattern is the wrong answer). LLMs including o1 and Gemini scored below physicians and were overconfident.
numbers: 100 questions; 53% include a 'seek more information' option. Most LLMs under 50%; some at or below chance (under 20%). Best: Gemini-1.5-Pro 50%, o1 48%. Five-physician human average with standard error 5.3 points.
limits: Only 100 items and 5 physicians; items are adversarial by design, so not a measure of everyday clinical skill (authors say so).
agent_relevance: Early (2025) baseline that newer work compares against; confirms fixation by pattern in language models and high confidence in wrong answers.

source: Shidara, Prem, Kim, Podlasek, Liu, Alaa, Bernardo (2026) Advances in LLM Reasoning Enable Flexibility in Clinical Problem-Solving (mARC)
finding: A year later, strong reasoning models reach physician-level accuracy on the same Einstellung benchmark, and beat physicians on the items physicians most often miss.
numbers: Five physicians mean 0.66 (95% CI 0.55-0.75). Best model Claude 4.1 Opus 0.751 (CI 0.738-0.763), mean of 15 runs; Gemini 2.5-Pro, GPT-5.1 and Grok-4-Fast-Reasoning not significantly different from humans. Human-miss set: 20 of 100 items, physicians 36% vs 73% elsewhere; Claude 4.1 Opus confidently correct on 55.0% of those items, confidently wrong on 25.0%.
limits: Only 5 physicians; 20-item subset; Wilson 90% intervals wide ([39.9, 80.0]). Contrasts with MedEinst (2026), where frontier models still show 43-61% trap rates, so results depend on benchmark design.
agent_relevance: Mixed evidence: long reasoning can override the familiar pattern, but not reliably. Reasoning effort is a lever for S1/O6.

source: Jiang, Ilievski, Ma, Sourati (2023) BRAINTEASER: Lateral Thinking Puzzles for Large Language Models
finding: 1,100 multiple-choice lateral thinking puzzles (sentence and word puzzles) where the default commonsense reading is the trap. Models stay far below humans and are inconsistent under rewording, hinting at memorisation.
numbers: ChatGPT scored about 53% and 63% (two subtasks) vs random 25% and human 92% (102 puzzles, 3 experts). ChatGPT sentence puzzles: original 60.77, semantic rewrite 59.33, context rewrite 67.94. About a third of models were at or below random.
limits: Multiple-choice format; ChatGPT may have seen some word puzzles (it answered 'The question seems to be a brain teaser'). Older models.
agent_relevance: Reconstruction (same puzzle, new wording) is a good guard against memorised answers when we test fixation breaking (G3).

source: Chen, Zhang, Wang, Wu (2024) Weak-eval-Strong: Evaluating and Eliciting Lateral Thinking of LLMs with Situation Puzzles (SPLAT)
finding: Situation puzzles (a short odd story; ask yes/no questions to find the hidden frame) tested as a multi-turn player-judge game. Using the benchmark's reasoning process as prompting data lifts other lateral-thinking sets.
numbers: 975 puzzles, 3 difficulty levels; judge agrees with humans over 80%. GPT-4 average accuracy about 41.7 as player. Llama3-70B on BrainTeaser improved from 71.20 to 79.54 overall with SPLAT-style reasoning; GPT-4 from 64.39 to 69.69. RiddleSense: Llama3-70B 83.34 to 85.21.
limits: Judge is itself an LLM; gains come from training or prompting on related puzzle-style data, so may reflect format learning.
agent_relevance: Interactive question-asking to surface the hidden frame is a candidate operator for O6; a judge with a reference story avoids self-grading (G5).

source: Ismayilzada et al. (2026) CresOWLve: Benchmarking Creative Problem-Solving Over Real-World Knowledge
finding: 2,061 puzzles from the quiz game 'What? Where? When?' that need creative insight plus facts. Models can fetch the facts but fail to make the non-obvious link.
numbers: Factual-vs-creative accuracy drop on the English set: -6.08% (Gemini-3.1-Pro high) to -17.21% (Mistral-Large-3-675B). Higher reasoning effort raised score monotonically within a model (GPT-5.4 nearly doubles with more effort).
limits: No formal human test; all items solved at least once by expert human teams (implicit 100% upper bound, not matched). Judge is an LLM.
agent_relevance: Retrieval is not the bottleneck; restructuring is. Supports spending budget on reframing rather than more retrieval.

source: Yang, Jangra, Muresan (2026) CREATE: Creativity Evaluation of VLMs using the Visual Remote Associates Test
finding: Visual Remote Associates puzzles. Models answer with the literal content of one image, which the authors read as fixation-like commitment to the first connection. Giving the cue words as text removes most of the gap.
numbers: 155 problems; human study N=25 on an 80-problem subset: 16.5% solved on first attempt, 22.8% by third. Only Claude-Opus-5.5 beat humans (32.5%); next best 12.5%. Text-only cues raised every model by 30.0-66.3 points (Claude-Opus-5.5 reached 90.0%). 22.8% of wrong model answers described the images literally vs 8.9% of human wrong guesses. Models answered every puzzle; humans gave up on 37.5%.
quote: models are more likely to commit to the first surface-level connection they find
limits: Model names are post-2025 versions I cannot independently check; humans are few and variable (5 people gave 49% of correct answers). Fixation reading is the authors' interpretation.
agent_relevance: Models never say 'I have no answer', so an impasse detector must be code (G1) rather than model self-report.

source: Zhang, Li, Peng, Sun, Guo, Hu, Chen, Zhao (2025) AI Delivers Creative Output but Struggles with Thinking Processes
finding: GPT models beat humans on some classic insight puzzles (character riddles, stumpers, rebus) but are clearly worse at the representational-change step itself. High scores may come from non-insight routes such as memory.
numbers: Rebus: humans below GPT-4-turbo by 0.32 and GPT-4o by 0.39 in accuracy (p<0.001). Chinese character puzzles: humans above GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 (0.09 each) but below GPT-4o (0.21). Stumpers: humans above GPT-3.5 (0.20) and GPT-4 (0.06), below GPT-4o (0.06).
limits: Only OpenAI models; one prompt per task, no prompt variants (authors cite budget). Chinese-language human samples (about 60-100 per experiment). Puzzles may be in training data.
agent_relevance: Beware contamination: high puzzle accuracy does not show restructuring. Test the process, not only the answer.

source: Zhang, Li, Peng, Sun, Guo, Hu, Chen, Zhao (2025) AI Delivers Creative Output but Struggles with Thinking Processes
finding: Representational change task (choose the option that reflects a new view of a rebus): humans win, and use 'transformation' while models use 'reasoning by deduction'.
numbers: Humans higher than GPT-4-turbo by 0.46 (95% CI 0.41-0.51) and GPT-4o by 0.31 (0.25-0.36), p<0.001. Strategy use: GPT-4o 68.88% and GPT-4-turbo 71.26% chose by reasoning; humans 72.41% by transformation.
limits: Strategy labels come from self-explanations, which may not reflect the true process (see SCHEMA note on written reasoning).
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that the missing piece in models is restructuring the representation, which is O6's job.

source: d'Aliberti and Horta Ribeiro (2026) The Illusion of Insight in Reasoning Models
finding: Mid-reasoning 'Wait, let's re-evaluate' shifts in RL-trained models are rare and do not usually raise accuracy. They look like unstable inference, not Kohler-style insight.
numbers: 1M+ traces, 3 domains (cryptic crosswords, MATH-500, Rush Hour), Qwen2.5 and Llama GRPO checkpoints. Shifts in 6.31% of traces overall (about 7.6% in one pool). Shifts did not become more frequent over training.
limits: Small models, GRPO runs of about 500 steps; shift detection uses lexical and structural cues with LLM annotation.
agent_relevance: Do not read the word 'Wait' as a reframe. The impasse trigger must be a code-measured signal.

source: d'Aliberti and Horta Ribeiro (2026) The Illusion of Insight in Reasoning Models
finding: Triggering a reconsideration cue from outside, only when token entropy is high, raises accuracy. This is an external impasse detector plus reframe, close to our G1 and O6.
numbers: Entropy-gated extrinsic reconsideration: +8.41 percentage points on MATH-500, smaller gains on crosswords and Rush Hour; effect of natural shifts varied with decoding temperature (0, 0.05, 0.3, 0.7).
limits: Gain measured on small open models; the cue is a generic reconsideration prompt, not a specific reframing operator.
agent_relevance: Strongest direct support in this angle for 'doubt only on a signal' (G1) with a code-measured signal.

source: Liang et al. (2023) Encouraging Divergent Thinking in LLMs through Multi-Agent Debate (MAD)
finding: Names the 'Degeneration-of-Thought' problem: once the model is confident in an answer, self-reflection cannot generate a new view even when the answer is wrong. This is fixation in an LLM loop. A debate with a judge partly breaks it.
numbers: Counter-Intuitive Arithmetic Reasoning (200 questions): GPT-3.5-Turbo 26.0%, +CoT 28.0, +Self-Consistency 29.5, +Self-Reflect 27.5, +MAD 37.0; GPT-4 51.0. Diversity: Self-Reflect 19.3 vs MAD 49.7 (bias 29.0 vs 24.8). Translation: MAD with GPT-3.5 beat GPT-4 on automatic and human scores.
limits: Debaters and judge are the same model family, so G4 applies (not independent). Small test sets; GPT-3.5 era.
agent_relevance: Self-reflection alone does not break fixation (consistent with G2). Forced diversity helps, but verification must be external.

source: Chen, Song, Zheng, Jing, Hansen, Sun (2025) Understanding Design Fixation in Generative AI
finding: Argues LLM and image models show design fixation: repeated themes, little contextual variation, bias to high-frequency words. Compares ChatGPT chair-design text with Red Dot award designs.
numbers: 10 designers (ages 20-26) used ChatGPT. Proportion of novel terms: ChatGPT 67.4% vs Red Dot human designs 78.2%. Unique words: Red Dot 312 vs ChatGPT 180; shared 86. Example: a 'cloud' theme drifted to tech-office chairs.
limits: Small qualitative sample; word-count novelty is a crude metric; single model (ChatGPT).
agent_relevance: Fixation here is homogenisation. Supports forcing different frames across attempts instead of resampling the same prompt.

source: Wadinambiarachchi, Kelly, Pareek, Zhou, Velloso (2024) The Effects of Generative AI on Design Fixation and Divergent Thinking
finding: Human experiment on AI as a source of fixation: people shown AI-generated example images fixated more on the example and produced fewer, less varied, less original ideas than a baseline.
numbers: Between-participants, N=60 (baseline, image search, GenAI). Bayesian models: GenAI negative on fluency (estimate about -0.21), variety effect small and negative (-0.15, 89% CI includes zero), originality negative with about 97% probability.
limits: Avatar-sketch task; effect sizes small with wide intervals; tests exposure to examples, not an LLM solver.
agent_relevance: Warns that showing the agent an example, or its own earlier attempt, may itself induce fixation. Keep attempts blind to each other (G4).

source: Xu, Martelaro, McComb (2026) Supervising Ralph Wiggum: Metacognitive Co-Regulation Agentic AI Loop for Engineering Design
finding: LLM design agents in a plain retry loop can fixate on one paradigm. Adding a metacognitive co-regulation agent that reviews design history (improving, stalling, regressing) gave better designs at the same step count.
numbers: Battery-pack design, 30 runs per system. Mean capacity: CRDAL 141.17 Ah vs plain loop 106.08 Ah (t(39.4)=7.174, p<0.001, d=1.846); CRDAL vs self-regulation loop (SRL) d=0.746. No significant difference in design steps. Best single design 192.50 Ah came from SRL.
limits: One task, one domain. Text reports SRL mean 72.07 Ah yet also says SRL beat the plain loop (d=0.956): an internal inconsistency to check before citing. Fixation itself is not measured directly.
agent_relevance: A separate monitor that reads the trajectory and flags stalling matches S1's impasse detector. The monitor, not the actor, decides.

source: Jeon, Cho, Shu (2025) PPoGA: Predictive Plan-on-Graph with Action for Knowledge Graph QA
finding: Built explicitly to fix 'functional fixedness' of planning agents: the agent can discard and rewrite the whole plan, not only repair a path.
numbers: GrailQA overall 78.9 vs predecessor PoG 76.5 (zero-shot split 82.3 vs 81.7); CWQ 64.5, WebQSP 83.1 (Hits@1, GPT-3.5 setting).
limits: Small gains; no ablation read isolating plan correction; gains may come from other parts of the system.
agent_relevance: A working example of plan-level versus path-level correction, matching O6 versus ordinary revision.

source: Liu, Karimnazarov, White (2025) Trapped by Expectations: Functional Fixedness in LLM-Enabled Chat Search
finding: Functional fixedness on the human side of an LLM: users carry over habits from search engines and voice assistants and under-use the chat model. Unmet expectations push them to adapt.
numbers: Crowd study N=450, six decision tasks, multi-prompt ChatGPT chats. Prior system experience shaped prompt language; failed expectations led to longer, more diverse prompts.
limits: Self-report plus prompt logs; not a performance test of an LLM, so only indirect.
agent_relevance: The user's framing also constrains the agent. S1 should restate the task in its own words.

source: Hao, Alexandre, Yu (2025) Visual LLMs Exhibit Human-Level Cognitive Flexibility in the Wisconsin Card Sorting Test
finding: Set-shifting (WCST, the classic perseveration measure) depends heavily on prompt and input. Without reasoning, models stay stuck; with chain-of-thought and text input they match or beat humans.
numbers: Categories completed: standard prompt, text input 0.3-0.5 across models; chain-of-thought, text input 4.6-5.0; human 4.73 (SD 0.45). Perseverative error counts did not fall uniformly (15.9 for one model under CoT text).
limits: WCST-64 variant; 3 models; 10 runs; model-to-row mapping in the PDF table is partly unclear.
agent_relevance: Written step-by-step reasoning plus clean text input is a large lever for set shifting. Image or vague inputs hide it.

source: de Langis et al. (2025) Strong Memory, Weak Control: Executive Functioning in LLMs
finding: Large working memory in LLMs does not predict control. Models fail inhibition tasks and show cognitive flexibility deficits.
numbers: Flanker incongruent trials: LLM accuracy 40-60% vs human 93-96%. Most LLMs exceed normative human working-memory scores.
limits: Task formats adapted for text; the link to fixation is inferential.
agent_relevance: Inhibiting the automatic response is the weak capacity, so it should sit in code, not be asked of the model (SCHEMA section 1).

source: Laban, Hayashi, Zhou, Neville (2025) LLMs Get Lost in Multi-Turn Conversation
finding: Models commit early, build on their own first answer, and do not recover when it was wrong. This is an anchoring and commitment form of fixation in conversations.
numbers: Average 39% drop from single-turn to multi-turn across six tasks; 200,000+ simulated conversations; aptitude loss minor but unreliability up 112%. Snowball repetition recovers only 15-20% of the drop (GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini).
quote: when LLMs take a wrong turn in a conversation, they get lost and do not recover
limits: Underspecified instructions are the trigger, not a puzzle trap; measures commitment, not insight.
agent_relevance: Premature commitment is costly; dropping the first attempt's context before a retry may be safer than repeating it.

source: Gu and Shi (2025) Diagnosing Shortcut-Induced Rigidity in Continual Learning: Einstellung Rigidity Index
finding: Borrows Einstellung for neural network training: shortcut features from earlier tasks slow later learning. Defines three measures: adaptation delay, performance deficit, relative suboptimal-feature reliance.
numbers: Two-phase CIFAR-100 with a spurious magenta patch; compared SGD, online EWC, DER++, GPM, deep generative replay. Continual-learning methods reached accuracy thresholds earlier (negative delay) but ended slightly lower on patched classes; masking the patch helped them.
limits: Image classification, not language; here the patch acted as a distractor rather than a helpful shortcut. Analogy only.
agent_relevance: Mechanism-level view: prior weights reuse the easiest cue. Not directly usable in a scaffold.

source: Bilalic, McLeod, Gobet (2008) Why good thoughts block better ones: the pernicious Einstellung effect (Cognition 108)
finding: Human mechanism result that LLM work borrows. Expert chess players who had found a familiar solution said they were looking for a better one, yet eye movements stayed on features of the familiar solution.
numbers: Record read: abstract only, via Europe PMC (PMID 18565505). No numbers taken from it. Paper is not open access.
limits: Full text not opened; abstract only.
agent_relevance: Saying 'still searching' is not proof of search; the agent should check that new attempts differ in structure from the first (G3).

source: Friston, Da Costa, Tschantz, Heins, Buckley, Verbelen, Parr (2025) Active inference and artificial reasoning
finding: A computational model of insight: the 'three-ball' task treats an aha moment as Bayesian model reduction that selects a rule after information-seeking actions. Used as an artificial-insight demo.
numbers: Discrete partially observed model; 81 possible likelihood mappings between latent states and feedback in the three-ball paradigm. No human data compared here.
limits: Technical note with synthetic agents only; not tested on language models.
agent_relevance: Insight framed as choosing between competing structural hypotheses by information gain; relevant to O6 and to naming the hypothesis space in S1.

source: Yang, Wu, Chen, Xiao, Yang, Wong, Wang (2025) Understanding Aha Moments: from External Observations to Internal Mechanisms
finding: Studies the R1-style 'aha moment' by language patterns, uncertainty and latent-space analysis. Reports more self-reflective, human-like tone and a shift in the model's perceived difficulty.
numbers: Qualitative and probe analyses; no single headline accuracy gain taken from the text read.
limits: Later work (Illusion of Insight, 2026) finds such shifts rarely help; this paper does not test accuracy effects as strongly.
agent_relevance: Treat an 'aha' tone as an uncertain signal; use measurable uncertainty instead.
